title: After an elementary etale extension, a finite type algebra splits into a finite factor and a factor with no quasi-finite point over the chosen prime
statement: Let $R \to S$ be a ring map of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], and let $\mathfrak p \subset R$ be a prime ideal. Then there are an etale ring map $R \to R'$ [def-weil-etale-morphism], a prime ideal $\mathfrak p' \subset R'$ lying over $\mathfrak p$ such that the induced map $\kappa(\mathfrak p) \to \kappa(\mathfrak p')$ is an isomorphism [def-weil-residue-field], and $R'$-algebras $A'$ and $B'$ with an $R'$-algebra isomorphism $R' \otimes_R S \cong A' \times B'$, such that $A'$ is a finitely generated $R'$-module and $R' \to B'$ is not quasi-finite [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] at any prime ideal of $B'$ lying over $\mathfrak p'$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK (lemma-etale-makes-quasi-finite-finite, lines 40362-40420), with the finitely many finite factors A_1,...,A_n combined as A' = product_i A_i

proof.text: *Fibre and induction parameter.* Put $F=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The base change is a finitely generated $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebra, so its isolated spectrum points form a finite set by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-field-finite-isolated-points]. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection], these points correspond to primes of $S$ over $\mathfrak p$, and by [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] they are exactly the primes where $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at the prime. We prove the assertion by induction on an upper bound $N$ for their number.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK, proof lines 40362-40420: finite isolated points in the finite-type fibre

proof.text: *Base case.* If $N=0$, take $R'=R$, $\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak p$, $A'=0$, and $B'=S$. The identity is etale, the residue-field map is the identity, and $R'\otimes_RS\cong0\times S$. The finite factor is finite, and the last assertion is exactly the absence of isolated fibre points in the definition [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK, proof lines 40362-40420: empty quasi-finite locus

proof.text: *One isolated point.* Assume $N>0$ and choose an isolated prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ over $\mathfrak p$. Applying [lem-weil-pbc-etale-quasi-finite-finite-one-prime] gives an etale map $R\to R_1$, a prime $\mathfrak p_1$ over $\mathfrak p$ with $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong\kappa(\mathfrak p_1)$, an idempotent $e$ in $C=R_1\otimes_RS$, and a prime $\mathfrak r$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ with $e\notin\mathfrak r$, such that $C_e$ is finite over $R_1$, $\mathfrak r$ is the unique prime over $\mathfrak p_1$ not containing $e$, and its contraction to $S$ is $\mathfrak q$. Let $D=C_{1-e}$. Then $C\cong C_e\times D$, and $R_1\to D$ is finite type by base change and localization.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK, proof lines 40362-40420, applying Lemma 00UJ to one isolated fibre prime

proof.text: *The count drops.* The residue-field isomorphism identifies the fibre of $C$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ with $F$, and [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection] transports the topology and isolatedness. Primes of $D=C_{1-e}$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ correspond to primes of $C$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ containing $e$, since a prime contains one of the orthogonal idempotents $e$ and $1-e$. The selected prime $\mathfrak r$ has $e\notin\mathfrak r$, so it lies in the $C_e$ factor and not in $D$. Thus the fibre of $R_1\to D$ has at most $N-1$ isolated points.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK, proof lines 40362-40420: the idempotent factor removes the selected isolated point

proof.text: *Induction and assembly.* Apply the induction hypothesis to $R_1\to D$ and $\mathfrak p_1$, obtaining an etale $R_1\to R_2$, a prime $\mathfrak p_2$, and $R_2$-algebras $A_2,B_2$ with $R_2\otimes_{R_1}D\cong A_2\times B_2$, $A_2$ finite, and $R_2\to B_2$ non-quasi-finite over $\mathfrak p_2$. Tensor $C\cong C_e\times D$ along $R_1\to R_2$ and use [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-product-distributes-product] to obtain $R_2\otimes_RS\cong(R_2\otimes_{R_1}C_e)\times A_2\times B_2$. Set $A'=(R_2\otimes_{R_1}C_e)\times A_2$ and $B'=B_2$. The first factor is finite because $C_e$ is finite and finite modules remain finite after base change; a finite product of finite modules is finite. The composite $R\to R_2$ is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-composition-cancellation], and the residue-field isomorphisms compose.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00UK, proof lines 40362-40420: induction, tensoring, and combining finite factors

proof.text: *The complementary factor.* Since $B'=B_2$, every prime of $B'$ over $\mathfrak p_2$ is non-quasi-finite by the induction hypothesis, which is the required final clause. This completes the induction and combines all finite factors into the single finite algebra $A'$.

split_report.summary: Split Algebra Lemma 00UK by induction on the finite set of isolated points in the finite-type fibre. The base case is the empty finite factor; the induction step applies the reviewed 00UJ one-point etale/idempotent decomposition, removes the selected isolated point from the complementary factor, applies the induction hypothesis, and combines finite factors after a further etale base change using the Mathlib tensor-product product equivalence. The fibre comparison and non-quasi-finite conclusion are explicit.
